Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Local spatial association and emerging hotspots, January 2021 to September 2025

Author

JUNCHEN LI

Published

October 18, 2026

1 Research question and scope

Where do recorded armed-conflict events and reported fatalities cluster across Myanmar townships, and how did local concentrations evolve between January 2021 and September 2025?

The analysis distinguishes absolute burden, spatial association, and temporal change in clustering. A large count does not by itself establish a statistically significant hotspot. A hotspot does not establish why violence occurred. The intended use is retrospective peace-building and humanitarian situational awareness at township level, not targeting, tactical planning, or individual risk prediction.

This report follows the Take-home Exercise 2 brief. The companion executive summary presents the central findings. All outputs below derive from the supplied data rather than textbook example numbers.

2 Data and study design

2.1 Sources and variables

Input Role Version and coverage
data/Aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv Local ACLED extract for the course exercise 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025
data/Geospatial/mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1.shp and companions Township boundaries obtained through MIMU GeoNode 330 unique township P-codes; embedded PCode_V is 9.4

The CSV contains violent and non-violent event types. The primary operational definition retains Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians within Myanmar. Protests, riots and strategic developments are excluded. This is an armed-conflict subset, not every event in ACLED’s broader political-violence category. The latter can include specific protest and riot subtypes. See the ACLED Codebook.

Two outcomes are analysed: the number of retained records and the sum of their reported fatalities. Fatalities represent recorded estimates, not an independently verified death toll. No population denominator is supplied, so neither outcome estimates per-capita risk. A zero bin means no retained record in this extract; it does not prove the absence of violence or complete reporting.

The boundary download request is preserved in data/Geospatial/wfsrequest.txt. The local file confirms the required version through its attributes. The source does not independently establish that every boundary reflects conditions in every study month. No download date is inferred from a file modification timestamp.

The course brief identifies eLearn as the distribution channel for its ACLED dataset. This report records the supplied filename and input fingerprint, but the local CSV alone does not verify its acquisition channel or download date. These provenance details require the original download record. The three retained event categories operationalise armed conflict consistently throughout the analysis.

2.2 Data-quality checks and spatial assignment

The preparation script checks IDs, dates, coordinates, non-negative fatalities, boundary validity and township identifiers. It repairs geometries if necessary and transforms both polygons and points to a WGS84 Albers equal-area CRS centred on Myanmar. Coordinates are assigned through polygon intersection rather than joining potentially ambiguous township names. Repeated place names remain distinct through their P-codes.

Invalid polygons repaired 0
Townships 330
Months 57
Township-month bins 18,810

There are 8 unassigned eligible records, all within one kilometre of the boundary. The primary analysis excludes these rather than silently snapping them. A sensitivity analysis assigns only these near-boundary records to their nearest polygon. Raw data remain unchanged. The main panel contains 53,992 events and 89,220 reported fatalities.

Geographic precision is not a distance-error estimate. The precise-location-only sensitivity retains code 1 and compares results with the full analysis. Among matched records, 107 lack admin3; 530 have a township name that differs under a simple case-insensitive comparison. These flags can reflect transliteration, coding or location discrepancies. They are not automatically treated as incorrect spatial matches. Temporal precision limitations remain relevant even after monthly aggregation.

2.3 Resolving the township-name flags

The initial string comparison is a screening device. Removing punctuation and spaces resolves 522 of the 530 non-missing name flags. A further four records use Pangsang, the primary name in the boundary label Pangsang (Panghkam), within the same state. These are compatible labels, not demonstrated changes of township. Four records instead name a different, uniquely identified township in the same state. The 107 missing names remain a separate quality category. These classifications use only the supplied boundary names and state labels; no fuzzy spelling match or unsupported external crosswalk is used.

2.3.1 Does the uncertainty change the static findings?

Three checks exclude the 111 unresolved/missing-name records, exclude all 637 initial flags (including harmless formatting differences), or assign the four conflicting records to their uniquely matched labels. Each check recomputes both outcomes with the original weights, seeds and 4,999 permutations. This is a targeted diagnostic of label uncertainty; it does not establish the correct location of an individual incident.

Show code 
kable(h$audit_counts,col.names=c('Scenario','Retained records','Excluded','Reassigned'))
Scenario Retained records Excluded Reassigned
Exclude unresolved or missing labels 53881 111 0
Exclude every initial name flag 53355 637 0
Use unique conflicting labels instead of coordinates 53992 0 4

kable(h$audit_stability,digits=3,
 col.names=c('Scenario','Outcome','Baseline BH hot','Alternative BH hot','Retained','Gained','Lost','Jaccard','BH LISA changes'))
Scenario Outcome Baseline BH hot Alternative BH hot Retained Gained Lost Jaccard BH LISA changes

All three scenarios retain the same 23 event and 27 fatality positive Gi* townships after BH adjustment. Their hotspot-set Jaccard similarity is 1.000. The separate LISA-change column prevents hotspot agreement from being mistaken for agreement on every local statistic. This materially narrows the original concern: the flagged names do not drive these adjusted static hotspot sets. It does not validate every input record or establish EHSA robustness to reassignments. Aggregate diagnostics are saved without incident IDs, coordinates or narrative notes.

2.4 A complete monthly space-time cube

The panel is the Cartesian product of 330 townships and 57 months: 18,810 bins. A left join of observed aggregates followed by explicit zero-filling prevents inactive townships or months from disappearing. Assertions reconcile panel totals with the matched input records. The study ends in September 2025; full-year totals for 2025 would not be comparable with earlier full years.

3 Descriptive geography

Recorded burden is uneven. Monywa (Sagaing); Kawkareik (Kayin); Myaing (Magway) have the largest event totals. The maps use a logarithmic colour transformation to show lower-count areas alongside large totals; the underlying counts are untransformed. Differences between event and fatality distributions can arise from the severity and composition of recorded incidents. These maps describe burden without testing clustering or controlling for population, land area, access or reporting intensity.

The peak event month is November 2023, with 1,473 records. The peak reported-fatality month is November 2023. The separate axes avoid treating different units as interchangeable. National changes can affect a space-time statistic with a pooled temporal reference, so township trend findings require comparison with this common temporal context.

The ranking identifies places contributing most to the recorded national burden. It is useful for selecting case studies for contextual review, but does not rank residents’ risk. A township can have a large total without being surrounded by similarly high-count neighbours; Local Moran’s I below separates those situations.

4 Spatial weights and inference

Queen contiguity represents shared boundaries or vertices, with a ten-metre tolerance after projection. Local Moran’s I excludes the focal township; Gi* includes it. Row-standardised weights give each neighbourhood total weight one. A township with no queen neighbour receives a reciprocal link to its nearest representative point so it can participate in analysis. This exception is explicit and does not imply a transport connection across water.

Show code 
kable(data.frame(Measure=c('Minimum analysis neighbours','Median analysis neighbours','Maximum analysis neighbours','Queen isolates repaired','Original connected components','Analysis connected components'),Value=c(min(s$weights$analysis_neighbours),median(s$weights$analysis_neighbours),max(s$weights$analysis_neighbours),sum(s$weights$isolate_link_added),s$queen_components,s$analysis_components)))
Measure Value
Minimum analysis neighbours 1
Median analysis neighbours 5
Maximum analysis neighbours 11
Queen isolates repaired 3
Original connected components 4
Analysis connected components 1

Different graph components are retained rather than joined arbitrarily. Conditional permutations still use the national reference distribution. A symmetric six-nearest-neighbour graph provides a sensitivity check. Neither graph is a causal model of conflict diffusion.

Static tests use 4,999 conditional permutations and two-sided simulation p-values, a fixed seed and one core. Their null concerns spatial arrangement conditional on observed values and the selected neighbourhood. Local Moran categories combine the test with the signs of the centred focal value and spatial lag. Gi* uses self-including weights. The spdep documentation specifies this distinction.

Main maps colour only tests with p < 0.05, as requested. Grey polygons supply context, not a significant class. Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) adjusted values are reported separately for each outcome and test family. Spatial dependence and heavy-tailed counts limit simple inferential interpretations; significance is exploratory, not a causal or predictive guarantee.

Thin state/region outlines and selected labels on the main LMSA and EHSA maps provide geographic reference. These labels are not statistical findings and do not change the township unit of analysis. The case locator and neighbourhood maps identify the more detailed areas discussed later.

4.1 Global context and Moran scatterplots

This supplementary step adapts the Global Moran’s I workflow in Hands-on Exercise 5(1) and the centred scatterplot in Hands-on Exercise 5(2), based on the course’s Chapter 9 and Chapter 10. Hunan GDPPC is replaced by the two Myanmar township totals. The existing queen-based graph, isolate repairs, township order and row standardisation are retained; the focal township is excluded.

The null randomly reallocates the observed totals across the fixed national graph. Each outcome uses 9,999 permutations and a fixed seed, with the null statistics generated by moran.mc. To avoid a zero simulated p-value, the reported two-sided p is twice the smaller inclusive tail probability, capped at one; each tail is (1 + number of equally or more extreme simulations) / 10,000. This explicit finite-simulation convention replaces the function’s returned p-value. Holm adjustment covers these two global tests only, separately from the existing local BH families. Under random allocation the expected I is -1/329, not exactly zero. This is a supplementary overall check, not a prerequisite for local analysis or a replacement for EHSA.

Show code 
global_table <- global_moran$results %>%
  transmute(Outcome=ifelse(variable=='events','Event counts','Reported fatalities'),
            `Moran I`=round(I,4),`Null expectation`=round(null_expectation,4),
            `Permutation p`=sprintf('%.4f',permutation_p),
            `Holm p (2 tests)`=sprintf('%.4f',holm_p),Permutations=permutations)
kable(global_table)
Outcome Moran I Null expectation Permutation p Holm p (2 tests) Permutations
Event counts 0.4900 -0.003 0.0002 0.0004 9999
Reported fatalities 0.5581 -0.003 0.0002 0.0004 9999

Both outcomes show positive overall spatial association at the two-test Holm 0.05 threshold. The larger fatality I does not establish a statistically tested difference between outcomes. Population, reporting coverage and other spatial heterogeneity can violate the national exchangeability assumption; these are count-based associations, not per-capita risks or causal effects.

Each point is a township. The axes show its standardised total and the neighbour average of the same standardised variable. The line through the origin has slope I because the weights sum to 330. Colours distinguish descriptive quadrants; triangles identify existing local Moran BH q < 0.05 results. Quadrant membership alone does not establish significance. Both panels use the same axis scales and raw totals before standardisation.

4.1.1 Sensitivity to skewness and spatial weights

For each outcome, a two-by-two comparison crosses raw totals and log1p(total) with the original queen graph and a symmetric six-nearest-neighbour graph. The latter uses the same projected representative points as the existing local sensitivity analysis. Symmetrisation retains an edge selected by either township, so final degrees can exceed six. All graphs exclude self-neighbours and use row-standardised weights. The transformation retains zeros and reduces the influence of large totals, but changes the measured variable and does not adjust for population or reporting.

Each setting uses 9,999 permutations and the same outcome-specific seed. Holm adjustment jointly covers all eight outcome/setting tests, including the two original raw/queen tests. The earlier two-test adjusted values remain labelled separately; none is substituted into local or EHSA results.

Show code 
global_sensitivity <- global_moran$sensitivity
kable(global_sensitivity %>%
  transmute(Outcome=ifelse(variable=='events','Events','Fatalities'),
            Weights=graph,Scale=transform,`Moran I`=round(I,3),
            `Permutation p`=sprintf('%.4f',permutation_p),
            `Holm p (8 tests)`=sprintf('%.4f',holm_p_8)))
Outcome Weights Scale Moran I Permutation p Holm p (8 tests)
Events Queen Raw 0.490 0.0002 0.0016
Events Queen log1p 0.662 0.0002 0.0016
Events Symmetric 6-NN Raw 0.429 0.0002 0.0016
Events Symmetric 6-NN log1p 0.591 0.0002 0.0016
Fatalities Queen Raw 0.558 0.0002 0.0016
Fatalities Queen log1p 0.707 0.0002 0.0016
Fatalities Symmetric 6-NN Raw 0.491 0.0002 0.0016
Fatalities Symmetric 6-NN log1p 0.659 0.0002 0.0016

Positive association remains supported in 8 of 8 settings after eight-test Holm adjustment. Event-count I ranges from 0.429 to 0.662. Fatality I ranges from 0.491 to 0.707.

The direction and significance survive reduced count skewness and an alternative graph. Magnitudes change, so they should not be treated as directly comparable effect sizes across scales or weights. These related checks are not independent replications, do not prove that extreme observations have no influence, and do not validate local or temporal classifications. All eight simulated p-values reach the doubled-tail floor of 0.0002; the common adjusted value of 0.0016 reflects simulation resolution, not identical strength of evidence.

5 Local measures of spatial association

5.1 Event counts

At unadjusted p < 0.05, 37 townships form High-High clusters, 50 Low-Low clusters, 0 High-Low outliers and 2 Low-High outliers. High-High examples include Hpa-An (Kayin); Myawaddy (Kayin); Kyainseikgyi (Kayin). These categories compare a township with its neighbours, not with its own past. Low-Low clusters may reflect low recorded activity or weaker observation; they do not establish safety.

The Gi* test identifies 38 hot-spot and 52 cold-spot townships at p < 0.05. It measures local concentrations including the focal area, whereas Moran’s I distinguishes clusters from outliers. These two maps therefore answer related but different questions. A significant hotspot supports unusually high local recorded burden under this reference model, not an explanation of its causes. The largest regional concentration is Sagaing, containing 17 of these nominal event-count hot spots.

5.2 Reported fatalities

Reported fatalities produce 38 High-High clusters and 0 High-Low outliers at p < 0.05. High-High examples include Kyainseikgyi (Kayin); Falam (Chin); Hakha (Chin). Fatality-based association need not reproduce event-count association: a small number of severe incidents can strongly affect the sum. Uncertain fatality reporting and differences in incident severity are therefore central limitations.

The fatality Gi* test yields 43 hot-spot and 66 cold-spot townships. 33 townships are nominal hot spots under both outcomes. Agreement supports reviewing those areas across both frequency and recorded severity, but neither measure provides a population-adjusted estimate or an independently verified death toll. Sagaing contains the largest number: 22 nominal fatality hot spots.

6 Emerging hot spot analysis

6.1 Space-time neighbourhood and classification

For each township-month, the Gi* neighbourhood contains the focal township and its spatial neighbours in the current month and the preceding month. January 2021 has no earlier bin and uses its current-month neighbourhood only. This is a retrospective, one-lag specification, not a forecasting model. Row standardisation accounts for differing neighbourhood sizes. The reference is the complete study cube, so national temporal change can contribute to local trends.

Space-time Gi* uses 999 conditional permutations with the focal observation fixed. A compiled Rcpp helper samples distinct non-focal bins by rejection sampling, avoiding full-population shuffles for every sparse neighbourhood. The two-sided p-value is twice the smaller inclusive-tail count, with a plus-one correction, capped at one. This handles ties conservatively. The helper was checked against exhaustive enumeration on a small graph; its Gi* z-values are computed by spdep::localG. Significant positive and negative bins define hot and cold episodes. A Mann-Kendall test of each township’s 57 Gi* z-values measures monotonic change in clustering strength. Its tau is an ordinal association, not an events-per-month growth rate.

Sign-specific rules distinguish new, consecutive, intensifying, diminishing, persistent, historical, sporadic and oscillating patterns. For persistent/intensifying/diminishing patterns, at least 90% of bins must be significant in the same direction. The classification uses the versioned ArcGIS Pro 3.4 pattern definitions, implemented explicitly in R. In particular, a sporadic hot or cold spot must be significant in the same direction in September 2025, have an earlier same-sign episode, fewer than 90% same-sign bins, and no opposite-sign episode. Earlier intermittent episodes with a non-significant final bin do not qualify. This definition differs from older documentation that omitted the terminal requirement.

The R workflow follows these pattern definitions but uses its own permutation-based inference. It does not reproduce ArcGIS numerically. The primary maps use nominal bin p-values to make the exercise’s p < 0.05 threshold explicit. A separate sensitivity analysis classifies BH-adjusted bins, because the documented ArcGIS workflow uses multiple-testing correction. The two inference conventions must not be conflated.

The map additionally requires Mann-Kendall p < 0.05 and a recognised pattern. A persistent hotspot without a significant trend can therefore be present in the full results but grey on this significance-filtered map. That is an intentional distinction between persistent clustering and evidence of change.

The heatmap contrasts clustering strength through time for the twenty highest-count townships. Its colours show z-values rather than a significance mask. It helps distinguish sustained concentrations from brief episodes before looking at the final classifications. Selection by total burden means this view is illustrative rather than representative of all townships.

6.2 Event-count patterns

220 townships meet the unadjusted Mann-Kendall threshold; 60 also have a recognised EHSA pattern and appear in colour. Positive tau indicates increasing Gi* values, which can mean intensifying high-value clustering or weakening low-value clustering. Negative tau has the reverse interpretation. The class label and the sign of Gi* must therefore be read together.

6.3 Fatality patterns

220 townships meet the Mann-Kendall threshold for reported fatalities, of which 58 also have a recognised pattern. This map assesses changes in the spatial concentration of recorded fatalities. It does not estimate changes in casualty risk, and sharp episodes can influence the Gi* trajectory even when the broader pattern is not monotonic.

6.4 Pattern-by-pattern findings

Each row below is a short description of a displayed pattern, including its geographic examples. Counts refer to townships, not conflict events. Full classifications and test statistics are available in outputs/ehsa_statistics.csv.

Outcome Pattern Townships Examples
events Consecutive cold spot 1 Kutkai (Shan (North))
events Intensifying cold spot 2 Matman (Shan (North)); Mongping (Shan (East))
events Oscillating hot spot 17 Kawkareik (Kayin); Kyainseikgyi (Kayin); Budalin (Sagaing)
events Sporadic cold spot 34 Puta-O (Kachin); Kawa (Bago (East)); Hlegu (Yangon)
events Sporadic hot spot 6 Hlaingbwe (Kayin); Myawaddy (Kayin); Mogoke (Mandalay)
fatalities Intensifying cold spot 2 Dagon (Yangon); Wakema (Ayeyarwady)
fatalities Oscillating cold spot 1 Kutkai (Shan (North))
fatalities Oscillating hot spot 6 Shwegu (Kachin); Budalin (Sagaing); Dawei (Tanintharyi)
fatalities Sporadic cold spot 43 Sumprabum (Kachin); Machanbaw (Kachin); Bago (Bago (East))
fatalities Sporadic hot spot 6 Launglon (Tanintharyi); Yebyu (Tanintharyi); Mogoke (Mandalay)

New patterns appear only in the final significant bin. Consecutive patterns form a single terminal run of at least two months, with no earlier significant bin of the same sign. Intensifying and diminishing patterns show significant directional change within a long-standing hot/cold concentration. Historical patterns lose their significant terminal status after a high share of earlier significant bins. Oscillating patterns include an earlier opposite-sign episode and a significant final bin. Sporadic patterns recur intermittently, end in a significant same-sign bin and contain no opposite-sign episode. The explicit precedence is new, long-standing, consecutive, oscillating and sporadic. These rules summarise observed sequences rather than predict future conflict. Automated tests cover both signs, the 90% boundary and non-significant final months.

6.4.1 Event counts: Consecutive cold spot

This pattern covers 1 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (North) (1). A previously absent same-sign pattern forms an uninterrupted cold run at the end of the study. Its persistence beyond September 2025 is unknown. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 1 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.2 Event counts: Intensifying cold spot

This pattern covers 2 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (East) (1) and Shan (North) (1). At least 90% of months are cold and the Gi* trend becomes more negative. This is strengthening low-value clustering, not intensifying violence. Of these townships, 2 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 2 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.3 Event counts: Oscillating hot spot

This pattern covers 17 townships; the largest regional counts are Magway (4) and Tanintharyi (4). The terminal hot episode follows an earlier cold episode. This changing sign argues against describing the entire period as uniformly high-conflict. Of these townships, 10 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 15 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.4 Event counts: Sporadic cold spot

This pattern covers 34 townships; the largest regional counts are Yangon (20) and Shan (South) (6). Low-value clustering recurs intermittently and the final month is cold relative to the pooled reference. This is neither proof of safety nor necessarily a decline in absolute events. Of these townships, 22 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 32 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.5 Event counts: Sporadic hot spot

This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Kayin (2) and Shan (North) (2). High-value episodes recur intermittently and the final month is hot. This supports a terminal concentration, but not sustained intensification throughout the study. Of these townships, 5 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 6 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.6 Reported fatalities: Intensifying cold spot

This pattern covers 2 townships; the largest regional counts are Ayeyarwady (1) and Yangon (1). At least 90% of months are cold and the Gi* trend becomes more negative. This is strengthening low-value clustering, not intensifying violence. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 2 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.7 Reported fatalities: Oscillating cold spot

This pattern covers 1 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (North) (1). The terminal cold episode follows earlier hot clustering. This indicates a change in relative concentration, not demonstrated conflict resolution. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 1 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.8 Reported fatalities: Oscillating hot spot

This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Kachin (1) and Magway (1). The terminal hot episode follows an earlier cold episode. This changing sign argues against describing the entire period as uniformly high-conflict. Of these townships, 4 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 6 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.9 Reported fatalities: Sporadic cold spot

This pattern covers 43 townships; the largest regional counts are Yangon (30) and Ayeyarwady (5). Low-value clustering recurs intermittently and the final month is cold relative to the pooled reference. This is neither proof of safety nor necessarily a decline in absolute events. Of these townships, 38 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 40 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

6.4.10 Reported fatalities: Sporadic hot spot

This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Rakhine (2) and Tanintharyi (2). High-value episodes recur intermittently and the final month is hot. This supports a terminal concentration, but not sustained intensification throughout the study. Of these townships, 6 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 6 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

events 220 210 162 60

The darker areas retain statistical support after adjusting the static event-count Gi* family. Nominal-only areas deserve more cautious interpretation. BH adjustment is a useful sensitivity check, not a correction for geolocation errors, uneven reporting or a misspecified neighbourhood. The unadjusted task maps should not be described as confirmed findings merely because they satisfy p < 0.05.

7.2 Neighbourhood, geolocation and temporal dependence

Show code 
kable(s$sensitivity_summary,digits=3,col.names=c('Alternative','Moran class agreement','Gi* class agreement','Hot spots'))
Alternative Moran class agreement Gi* class agreement Hot spots
Add records within 1 km of boundary 1.000 1.000 38
Precisely located events only 0.927 0.927 38
Six-nearest-neighbour graph 0.858 0.836 41

Agreement compares all township labels, including non-significant ones, so it can be high even when some hotspots change. The six-nearest-neighbour graph tests the spatial definition; the precision-code-1 subset changes both location quality and sample composition; the one-kilometre reassignment tests the eight near-boundary exclusions. None is automatically a superior truth.

Neighbourhoods overlap in time and Gi* series can be serially correlated. The conventional Mann-Kendall p-value assumes temporal independence. The extended checks use 999 permutations each of consecutive 3-, 6- and 12-month blocks, preserving order within each block and comparing absolute tau. A shorter final block is retained when the width does not divide 57. The plus-one p-value has resolution 0.001. These checks assume blocks are exchangeable under the null. They do not fully correct seasonality, non-stationarity or long-range dependence. In particular, the 12-month version has only five blocks and limited distinct rearrangements.

This intersection is a conservative sensitivity screen, not a calibrated joint p-value or proof of persistence. Grey combines unrecognised patterns and non-significant trends, rather than certifying an absence of conflict.

The baseline includes the current and previous month. Alternative models use the current month only, or the current plus two preceding months. Each repeats the Gi* simulation and pattern classification using the same spatial graph and seed. A fourth comparison retains the baseline z-values but replaces bin p-values with BH q-values across all 18,810 bins, separately for each outcome. It does not adjust the MK family a second time.

8 Frequency, severity and additional spatial evidence

8.1 Do the two hotspot measures identify the same places?

21 townships are positive Gi* concentrations under both outcomes after separate BH adjustments; 2 qualify only for events and 6 only for fatalities. The distinction shows why event frequency alone can miss areas with relatively concentrated fatality burden. A difference between significance labels is not itself a statistically significant difference between the outcomes. Both tests reuse the same incident records, and the comparison remains descriptive. The four numbered locations are examined below.

8.2 Conditional spatial random-labelling of fatality severity

Additional question: Which local neighbourhoods have more reported fatalities than expected from their recorded event locations, months and event-type composition?

This extends the core count-based analyses through a conditional simulation. Each event keeps its township, month and type. Within each month-by-event-type stratum, fatality marks are randomly reassigned among the recorded events without replacement. The procedure preserves incident frequency, temporal patterns, type composition and each stratum’s entire fatality distribution. It breaks the association between location and severity within those strata.

The reference model adapts the grouped random-labelling principle documented in spatstat’s rlabel: locations stay fixed while marks are permuted within groups. Here, explicit R code computes an areal-neighbourhood statistic rather than a point-pattern summary function.

The statistic for each township is the fatality sum in its self-including queen neighbourhood. Its conditional expectation sums the month/type mean fatality mark over the events in that neighbourhood. The observed-to-expected ratio describes excess severity, not individual fatality risk. A one-sided upper-tail p-value uses 999 randomisations and a plus-one correction. BH adjusts the family of 330 township neighbourhoods. The complete analysis is repeated on precision-code-1 records, with expectations recalculated for that subset.

This is a random-labelling reference model, not a causal model. It assumes exchangeable fatality marks within each month/type stratum under the null. Reporting differences, actor composition and correlated incidents can violate that assumption. Overlapping neighbourhoods are dependent; the BH screen is exploratory and does not establish arbitrary-dependence control. The same underlying incidents can contribute to several neighbourhoods, so their totals must never be added together. The approach complements raw fatality hotspots by conditioning on recorded frequency and type.

53 neighbourhoods have excess fatality marks at BH q < 0.05; 21 also pass the independently rerun precision-code-1 analysis. Among full-data excess neighbourhoods, 32 are outside the ordinary fatality Gi* hotspot set after BH adjustment. These findings answer a conditional severity question that the raw-count maps do not. Examples with the largest observed-to-expected ratios include Kyangin (Ayeyarwady); Myanaung (Ayeyarwady); Padaung (Bago (West)). Each name identifies the focal township plus its neighbours. The result supports checking local incident composition and reporting before interpreting fatalities simply as a consequence of frequent events. Of these three examples, 0 retain q < 0.05 in the precise-only analysis, so the large ratios alone should not determine which places receive strongest emphasis.

Positive and negative contributions can offset, so a type’s share of net excess can exceed 100%. Reporting practices and correlated incidents remain alternative explanations.

The largest contributions occur in 2022 for Kyunhla and Taze, and in 2023 for Kawlin. This locates the periods to prioritise for contextual verification without claiming continuous escalation. No individual-incident details are displayed.

8.3.1 S1: Kyunhla neighbourhood

Across 9 townships, 1,830 retained incidents contain 4,929 reported fatalities against a conditional expectation of 3221.0. The O/E ratio is 1.53 (BH q = 0.013), increasing to 1.75 in the precision-code-1 analysis (q = 0.019). Battles contribute 1082.7 excess fatalities, or 63.4% of the net excess; 2022 supplies the largest calendar-period contribution. The single largest incident represents 3.6% of observed fatalities, while the largest month contributes 6.3%. These concentration checks describe leverage but do not replace a leave-one-out test. The focal township is not an ordinary BH-adjusted event or fatality hotspot. The added insight is therefore conditional severity beyond raw concentration. This supports checking incident composition and reporting in the neighbourhood, not a causal explanation or an assistance ranking.

8.4 Randomisation stability and largest-incident sensitivity

The three severity cases were fixed before these checks; no failed case is replaced. Each of three recorded seeds repeats the complete severity analysis with 1,999 permutations, separately for all assigned records and precision-code-1 records. BH adjustment always covers all 330 neighbourhoods, not only the selected three. Observed counts and O/E ratios stay fixed within each sample; only Monte Carlo p-values vary. The resulting q-value ranges describe simulation sensitivity, not confidence intervals.

Cases are selected by fixed contrast rules: the largest event total among displayed oscillating event hot spots, the largest among displayed sporadic event hot spots, the largest without a displayed event trend-pattern, and the largest fatality total among fatality-only BH hot spots. Already selected townships are excluded from subsequent slots, with P-code breaking ties. These illustrative cases are selected from the analysed data, not an independent validation sample or a claim to represent all Myanmar townships.

Each profile separates monthly counts from space-time Gi* values. The median of all pairwise monthly slopes (Sen’s slope) quantifies Gi* change in z-units per month and count change in events or reported fatalities per month. January–September 2024 and 2025 totals compare identical calendar windows, avoiding a partial-year versus full-year comparison.

10 Local change in the national context

10.1 A constant-share comparison

Raw-count EHSA uses a pooled space-time reference and can respond to nationwide change. The following diagnostic asks whether the four township profiles also gain or lose share of the recorded national total. For township i and period t, the share is its retained count divided by the sum across all 330 townships. The benchmark for January-September 2025 holds the township’s January-September 2024 share constant and multiplies it by the 2025 national total. Relative growth is (local 2025 / local 2024) / (national 2025 / national 2024); values above one indicate a share gain. A zero starting local total leaves that ratio undefined rather than introducing a pseudocount.

This is an accounting benchmark, not a fitted causal model, population-adjusted risk estimate or replacement EHSA. Shares are compositional and use the same potentially incomplete reporting system. Comparing the same nine months reduces unequal-duration and calendar-season differences, but cannot remove changes in reporting coverage. Quarterly shares below use all three months’ totals, not an average of monthly percentages.

kable(h$national_windows,digits=1,col.names=c('Outcome','Jan-Sep 2024','Jan-Sep 2025','National change %'))

fatalities 16879 11893 -29.5

National retained events fall from 9,975 to 8,749 between January-September 2024 and 2025 (12.3%). In contrast, Kawkareik’s events increase from 122 to 356 and its share rises from 1.22% to 4.07%; Nawnghkio increases from 202 to 341, with its share rising from 2.03% to 3.90%. Their matched-window increases therefore cannot be explained by an increasing national event total in that window. Monywa and Myingyan lose event share as well as counts. These comparisons strengthen the geographical interpretation while leaving the original full-period EHSA tests unchanged.

National reported fatalities decline by 29.5% in the matched windows. Kawkareik increases in both count and share. Nawnghkio’s count falls from 91 to 70, yet its national share rises slightly from 0.54% to 0.59%; Myingyan similarly falls from 428 to 313 while its share moves from 2.54% to 2.63%. Neither small share increase establishes a statistically significant increase. Monywa declines in both measures. Absolute decline and relative concentration can coexist, so a falling fatality count alone does not establish improvement relative to the national pattern.

The strongest supported statement is window-specific: Kawkareik and Nawnghkio gain event share during a national decline, while Monywa and Myingyan lose event share. This diagnostic does not show that national trends have been removed from all 57-month Gi* trajectories. Causal explanations and independent reporting validation remain outside the available evidence.

10.2 Contemporaneous humanitarian context

Nawnghkio, northern Shan. OCHA’s 28 March 2025 update, “Continued insecurity in the Northeast” describes repeated clashes and aerial attacks in Nawnghkio, including reported civilian casualties. This supplies contemporaneous context for examining its growing event share. It does not independently verify this report’s exact incident counts or explain why fatalities decline in the matched window. Humanitarian reporting and ACLED may also draw on overlapping underlying sources.

Kawkareik within Kayin. The same OCHA update, southeastern Myanmar discussion reports approximately 2,800 people displaced in Kayin since mid-February 2025, alongside conflict-related needs for food, medicine and relief items. This evidence is at state level, not an estimate for Kawkareik. It supports examining displacement and service access alongside the township’s increased recorded activity, but cannot allocate those displaced people to this case or establish a township-level causal explanation.

Implication for both cases. OCHA’s 23 September 2025 update identifies continued displacement and severe humanitarian-access constraints, particularly in the Northwest and Southeast. Accordingly, neither a national decline in recorded counts nor a local cold-spot label establishes falling humanitarian need. These sources fall within the study period. They are contextual evidence, not extra observations inserted into the statistical tests, and do not validate the selected Sagaing severity neighbourhoods’ 2022–2023 peaks.

11 Integrated interpretation and peace-building implications

The analysis separates where burden accumulated from whether local concentrations changed. Areas supported by both outcome measures, multiple-testing adjustment and sensitivity checks are stronger candidates for contextual review than areas identified by one nominal test alone. Event counts capture frequency, while reported fatalities add a severity perspective.

Sagaing contains the largest number of nominal static hot spots for both outcomes: 17 event-count hot spots and 22 fatality hot spots. The monthly peak for both measures is November 2023. However, the time-pattern maps are dominated by intermittent classes rather than intensifying hot spots. There are 6 sporadic and 17 oscillating event hot spots, compared with 6 and 6 for fatalities. Accumulated burden and persistent escalation are therefore not interchangeable findings.

Humanitarian interpretation should combine these results with independent information about displacement, access, health services and local reporting. Low observed activity must not justify withdrawing support from under-observed areas. Township aggregation is suitable for strategic discussion, but obscures variation within large townships and does not identify safe routes, individual exposure, perpetrators or causal mechanisms. No operational targeting recommendations follow from these maps.

Case evidence Implication for humanitarian assessment Information still needed
Kawkareik: recent recorded activity increases, but the long-block event trend check fails Review recent needs without describing the entire period as a stable escalation Reporting continuity, displacement and service availability during the matched windows
Nawnghkio: event counts increase while reported fatalities decrease in the matched windows Keep frequency and severity indicators separate when reviewing changing needs Incident composition, fatality reporting quality and independent local assessments
Monywa: large cumulative burden, declining matched-window counts and no displayed event pattern Retain accumulated harm in the assessment even when the temporal map is grey Unmet needs, recovery conditions and changes in observation coverage
Myingyan: fatality-only adjusted hotspot, with a recent decline despite a positive full-period Gi* slope Include recorded severity in contextual screening and avoid presenting a long-period slope as current growth Severe-incident details at an appropriate aggregate level and corroborating humanitarian evidence

Kyunhla, Kawlin and Taze add a complementary severity finding outside the ordinary adjusted count hotspots. Their decompositions point to battles and past concentrations, rather than uninterrupted recent escalation. These screens identify questions for local assessment; they do not prescribe resource allocation by statistical rank.

12 Limitations and conclusion

ACLED records depend on source availability and coding decisions. Locations and dates have varying precision; fatalities are uncertain. The fixed boundary vintage may not match all administrative changes during 2021–2025. Count-based association confounds population, area, reporting intensity and underlying conflict activity. Results also depend on temporal aggregation, weight definitions, multiplicity handling and the pooled space-time reference.

Three conclusions follow:

  • Overall association: positive Global Moran association survives all 8 tested scale/weight settings after eight-test Holm adjustment. Existing local tests identify where concentrations and contrasts occur.
  • Temporal change: only 14 of 60 event and 23 of 58 fatality displayed patterns pass the additional trend screen. National temporal confounding remains unresolved.
  • Conditional severity: the three selected neighbourhoods retain support across repeated seeds and largest-record deletion in both samples. Their overlapping neighbourhoods and data-driven selection preclude independent validation claims.

Together these findings support contextual investigation of burden, change and severity. They do not establish safe areas, causal diffusion or steadily intensifying conflict throughout Myanmar.

13 Reproducibility

Project repository: JUNCHENLI2026/ISSS626_GAA on GitHub. Exercise sources are organised under Take-Home_Ex/Take-Home_Ex02/.

The report and executive summary read the same analytical outputs. Raw inputs remain unchanged. From the exercise folder, run Rscript --vanilla analysis/run_analysis.R, then render the two QMD documents. Dependencies are checked rather than installed automatically; changed inputs, analysis scripts or package versions invalidate the relevant caches.

The technical appendix contains the complete analysis scripts, test and rebuild instructions, input fingerprints and runtime information. It is collapsed by default. Individual event notes and coordinates are not embedded in the reporting pages.

AI assistance was used to optimise parts of the R code and fix some bugs.

# Locale-independent English month labels for both reporting documents.
format_month_en <- function(x) {
  dates <- as.Date(x)
  labels <- paste(month.name[as.integer(format(dates, "%m"))],
                  format(dates, "%Y"))
  labels[is.na(dates)] <- NA_character_
  labels
}

Preparation code

 # Prepare a complete township-month panel without changing the raw files.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(sf);library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(readr);library(lubridate);library(spdep)})
dir.create('outputs',showWarnings=FALSE)
set.seed(20261018)
raw_paths <- c('data/Aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv', list.files('data/Geospatial',full.names=TRUE))
raw_hashes <- tools::md5sum(raw_paths)
raw <- read_csv(raw_paths[1],show_col_types=FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw$event_id_cnty))
raw$event_date <- as.Date(raw$event_date)
stopifnot(!anyNA(raw$event_date), all(raw$fatalities>=0), !anyNA(raw$fatalities))
event_types <- c('Battles','Explosions/Remote violence','Violence against civilians')
eligible <- raw %>% filter(country=='Myanmar',event_date>=as.Date('2021-01-01'),event_date<=as.Date('2025-09-30'),event_type %in% event_types)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(eligible$longitude)),all(is.finite(eligible$latitude)))
townships_raw <- st_read('data/Geospatial/mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1.shp',quiet=TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(townships_raw)==330,all(as.character(townships_raw$PCode_V)=='9.4'),!anyDuplicated(townships_raw$TS_PCODE))
invalid_before <- sum(!st_is_valid(townships_raw))
crs_area <- '+proj=aea +lat_1=10 +lat_2=28 +lat_0=19 +lon_0=96 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs'
townships <- townships_raw %>% st_make_valid() %>% st_transform(crs_area) %>% arrange(TS_PCODE)
stopifnot(all(st_is_valid(townships)),!any(st_is_empty(townships)))
townships$area_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(townships))/1e6
coords <- eligible %>% distinct(longitude,latitude)
pts <- st_as_sf(coords,coords=c('longitude','latitude'),crs=4326,remove=FALSE) %>% st_transform(st_crs(townships))
hits <- st_intersects(pts,townships)
coords$match_count <- lengths(hits)
coords$township_id <- vapply(hits,function(h) if(length(h)==1)townships$TS_PCODE[h] else NA_character_,character(1))
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(pts,townships)
coords$nearest_id <- townships$TS_PCODE[nearest]
coords$nearest_m <- as.numeric(st_distance(pts,townships[nearest,],by_element=TRUE))
events <- eligible %>% left_join(coords,by=c('longitude','latitude')) %>% mutate(month=as.Date(format(event_date,'%Y-%m-01')))
assigned <- events %>% filter(!is.na(township_id))
unassigned <- events %>% filter(is.na(township_id))
months <- seq(as.Date('2021-01-01'),as.Date('2025-09-01'),by='month')
panel <- expand_grid(township_id=townships$TS_PCODE,month=months) %>%
 left_join(assigned %>% group_by(township_id,month) %>% summarise(events=n(),fatalities=sum(fatalities),.groups='drop'),by=c('township_id','month')) %>%
 mutate(across(c(events,fatalities),~replace_na(.x,0))) %>% arrange(month,township_id)
stopifnot(nrow(panel)==330*57,sum(panel$events)==nrow(assigned),sum(panel$fatalities)==sum(assigned$fatalities),!anyDuplicated(panel[c('township_id','month')]))
totals <- panel %>% group_by(township_id) %>% summarise(events=sum(events),fatalities=sum(fatalities),active_months=sum(events>0),.groups='drop')
townships <- townships %>% left_join(totals,by=c('TS_PCODE'='township_id'))
audit <- tibble(stage=c('Input rows','Outside Myanmar','Outside requested dates','Other event types within Myanmar/time','Eligible armed-conflict records','Unique spatially assigned records','Unassigned or ambiguous records','Assigned reported fatalities','Invalid polygons repaired','Townships','Months','Township-month bins'),
 value=c(nrow(raw),sum(raw$country!='Myanmar'),sum(raw$event_date<min(months)|raw$event_date>as.Date('2025-09-30')),sum(raw$country=='Myanmar' & !(raw$event_type %in% event_types)),nrow(events),nrow(assigned),nrow(unassigned),sum(assigned$fatalities),invalid_before,nrow(townships),length(months),nrow(panel)))
precision <- assigned %>% count(geo_precision,time_precision,name='records')
name_check <- assigned %>% left_join(st_drop_geometry(townships) %>% select(TS_PCODE,TS),by=c('township_id'='TS_PCODE')) %>% summarise(missing_admin3=sum(is.na(admin3)),exact_name_disagreement=sum(!is.na(admin3)&tolower(trimws(admin3))!=tolower(trimws(TS))))
quality <- list(audit=audit,precision=precision,name_check=name_check,
 unmatched=unassigned %>% count(geo_precision,match_count,name='records'),
 near_boundary=sum(unassigned$match_count==0 & unassigned$nearest_m<=1000),
 event_types=raw %>% count(event_type,name='records'), hashes=raw_hashes)
saveRDS(list(townships=townships,panel=panel,assigned=assigned,unassigned=unassigned,months=months,quality=quality), 'outputs/prepared.rds')
write_csv(audit,'outputs/data_audit.csv')
print(audit,n=Inf);print(quality$unmatched);print(name_check)
cat('Unassigned within 1 km:',quality$near_boundary,'\n')

Statistical code

 # Local association and a one-month-lag space-time Gi* analysis.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(spdep);library(Kendall);library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(sf)})
d <- readRDS('outputs/prepared.rds')
g <- d$townships
n <- nrow(g); nt <- length(d$months)
set.seed(20261018)
spdep::set.coresOption(1L)
nb0 <- poly2nb(g,queen=TRUE,row.names=g$TS_PCODE,snap=10)
xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(g))
isolates <- which(card(nb0)==0L)
nb <- nb0
if(length(isolates)) {
  kn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=1))
  for(i in isolates) {j <- kn[[i]][1];nb[[i]]<-as.integer(j);nb[[j]]<-sort(unique(as.integer(c(nb[[j]][nb[[j]]>0],i))))}
}
lw <- nb2listw(nb,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
gstar_w <- nb2listw(include.self(nb),style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
kn6 <- make.sym.nb(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=6),row.names=g$TS_PCODE))
weights_audit <- data.frame(township=g$TS,code=g$TS_PCODE,queen_neighbours=card(nb0),analysis_neighbours=card(nb),isolate_link_added=seq_len(n)%in%isolates)
local_results <- function(x,w,star,seed=20261018,nsim=4999L) {
  mi <- localmoran_perm(x,w,nsim=nsim,alternative='two.sided',iseed=seed,no_repeat_in_row=TRUE,zero.policy=TRUE)
  gi <- localG_perm(x,star,nsim=nsim,alternative='two.sided',iseed=seed+1L,no_repeat_in_row=TRUE,zero.policy=TRUE)
  z <- as.numeric(scale(x)); lagz <- lag.listw(w,z,zero.policy=TRUE)
  pmi <- mi[,'Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim']; pgi <- attr(gi,'internals')[,'Pr(z != E(Gi)) Sim']
  tibble(Ii=mi[,'Ii'],moran_p=pmi,moran_q=p.adjust(pmi,'BH'),gi_z=as.numeric(gi),gi_p=pgi,gi_q=p.adjust(pgi,'BH'),
    lisa=ifelse(pmi<.05,ifelse(z>=0,ifelse(lagz>=0,'High-High','High-Low'),ifelse(lagz>=0,'Low-High','Low-Low')),'Not significant'),
    hotspot=ifelse(pgi<.05,ifelse(as.numeric(gi)>0,'Hot spot','Cold spot'),'Not significant'))
}
static <- bind_rows(lapply(c('events','fatalities'),function(v) bind_cols(tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE,variable=v),local_results(g[[v]],lw,gstar_w))))

# Time-major ordering: each monthly block contains the same 330 townships.
stnb <- vector('list',n*nt)
for(t in seq_len(nt)) for(i in seq_len(n)) {
  spatial <- sort(unique(c(i,nb[[i]][nb[[i]]>0])))
  here <- (t-1L)*n+i
  stnb[[here]] <- sort(as.integer(c((t-1L)*n+spatial,if(t>1L)(t-2L)*n+spatial else integer())))
}
class(stnb)<-'nb';attr(stnb,'region.id')<-as.character(seq_along(stnb));attr(stnb,'type')<-'space-time';attr(stnb,'sym')<-FALSE;attr(stnb,'self.included')<-TRUE
stw <- nb2listw(stnb,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
stopifnot(all(vapply(seq_along(stnb),function(i)i%in%stnb[[i]],logical(1))))

# Explicit, sign-specific pattern rules. No classification depends on place names.
classify_pattern <- function(z,p,tau,mkp) {
  hot<-p<.05 & z>0;cold<-p<.05 & z<0;m<-length(z)
  one_side <- function(a,opp,sign) {
    count<-sum(a);last<-a[m];share<-mean(a)
    if(count==0)return(NULL)
    if(last && count==1)return(paste('New',sign))
    if(share>=.9) {
      if(!last)return(paste('Historical',sign))
      if(mkp<.05) {
        growing <- if(sign=='hot spot') tau>0 else tau<0
        return(paste(if(growing)'Intensifying' else 'Diminishing',sign))
      }
      return(paste('Persistent',sign))
    }
    if(last) {
      run<-rle(rev(a))$lengths[1]
      if(run>=2 && run==count)return(paste('Consecutive',sign))
      if(any(opp))return(paste('Oscillating',sign))
    }
    # ArcGIS Pro 3.4 definitions require a same-sign significant final bin.
    if(last && !any(opp))return(paste('Sporadic',sign))
    NULL
  }
  a<-one_side(hot,cold,'hot spot');if(!is.null(a))return(a)
  a<-one_side(cold,hot,'cold spot');if(!is.null(a))return(a)
  'No pattern detected'
}
ehsa <- list(); gis <- list()
source('analysis/fast_gi.R')
for(v in c('events','fatalities')) {
  message('Space-time Gi*: ',v)
  x<-d$panel[[v]]
  gi<-fast_space_time_gi(x,stw,nsim=999L,seed=20261018L)
  zz<-gi$z; pp<-gi$p
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(zz)),all(is.finite(pp)),length(zz)==n*nt)
  gis[[v]]<-d$panel %>% select(township_id,month) %>% mutate(variable=v,gi_z=zz,p=pp,q=p.adjust(pp,'BH'))
  zm<-matrix(zz,nrow=n); pm<-matrix(pp,nrow=n)
  r<-lapply(seq_len(n),function(i) {
    mk<-MannKendall(zm[i,]); tau<-as.numeric(mk$tau); p<-as.numeric(mk$sl)
    if(!is.finite(p)){p<-1;tau<-0}
    # Three-month-block permutation preserves within-block temporal ordering.
    set.seed(20261018+i)
    blocks<-split(seq_len(nt),rep(seq_len(nt/3),each=3))
    obs<-tau
    null<-replicate(999,as.numeric(MannKendall(zm[i,unlist(blocks[sample(length(blocks))])])$tau))
    finite_null<-null[is.finite(null)]
    block_p<-if(length(finite_null)) (1+sum(abs(finite_null)>=abs(obs)))/(length(finite_null)+1) else 1
    tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE[i],variable=v,tau=tau,mk_p=p,block_p=block_p,hot_months=sum(pm[i,]<.05 & zm[i,]>0),cold_months=sum(pm[i,]<.05 & zm[i,]<0),
      final_gi=zm[i,nt],final_p=pm[i,nt],classification=classify_pattern(zm[i,],pm[i,],tau,p))
  })
  ehsa[[v]]<-bind_rows(r) %>% mutate(mk_q=p.adjust(mk_p,'BH'),map_class=ifelse(mk_p<.05 & classification!='No pattern detected',classification,'Not displayed'))
}
ehsa<-bind_rows(ehsa);gis<-bind_rows(gis)

# Sensitivity: alternative spatial neighbours, geolocation precision, and near-boundary records.
precise<-d$assigned %>% filter(geo_precision==1) %>% count(township_id)
x_precise<-replace_na(precise$n[match(g$TS_PCODE,precise$township_id)],0)
near<-d$unassigned %>% filter(match_count==0,nearest_m<=1000) %>% count(nearest_id)
x_near<-g$events+replace_na(near$n[match(g$TS_PCODE,near$nearest_id)],0)
sensitivity<-bind_rows(
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Six-nearest-neighbour graph',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(g$events,nb2listw(kn6,style='W'),nb2listw(include.self(kn6),style='W'))),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Precisely located events only',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(x_precise,lw,gstar_w)),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Add records within 1 km of boundary',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(x_near,lw,gstar_w)))
baseline<-static %>% filter(variable=='events')
sensitivity_summary<-sensitivity %>% group_by(scenario) %>% summarise(lisa_agreement=mean(lisa==baseline$lisa),hotspot_agreement=mean(hotspot==baseline$hotspot),hotspots=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot'),.groups='drop')
inference<-static %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(lisa_raw=sum(moran_p<.05),lisa_BH=sum(moran_q<.05),gi_raw=sum(gi_p<.05),gi_BH=sum(gi_q<.05),.groups='drop')
ehsa_summary<-ehsa %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(MK_raw=sum(mk_p<.05),MK_BH=sum(mk_q<.05),block_supported=sum(mk_p<.05 & block_p<.05),displayed=sum(map_class!='Not displayed'),.groups='drop')
saveRDS(list(static=static,ehsa=ehsa,gis=gis,weights=weights_audit,nb=nb,queen_components=n.comp.nb(nb0)$nc,analysis_components=n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
 sensitivity=sensitivity,sensitivity_summary=sensitivity_summary,inference=inference,ehsa_summary=ehsa_summary), 'outputs/statistics.rds')
write.csv(static,'outputs/local_statistics.csv',row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(ehsa,'outputs/ehsa_statistics.csv',row.names=FALSE)
print(inference);print(ehsa_summary);print(sensitivity_summary)
print(table(ehsa$variable,ehsa$map_class))
